subject: Communication
title: Listening Across Generations
description: A fast breakdown of Listening Across Generations for builders.

hook.text: 'Kids these days don't listen.' 'Boomers never hear us.' Every generation says this.

buildup.text: Different generations have different communication norms: formality levels, preferred channels, feedback expectations.

discovery.text: Gen Z prefers text and visual communication. Boomers prefer face-to-face.

twist.text: Research shows generational stereotypes are mostly overblown.

climax.text: Cross-generational listening requires curiosity, not assumptions. Ask 'how do you prefer to communicate?'

punchline.text: Generations don't have ears. People do. Listen to the person, not the label.

quiz.question: What does research show about generational communication differences?
options: Within-generation variation is larger than between-generation differences

details.summary: Each generation has distinct communication styles shaped by technology, culture, and historical events. Baby Boomers value face-to-face depth, Gen X prefers directness, Millennials favor collaborative dialogue, and Gen Z communicates through digital-native shorthand.
details.whyItMatters: Generational listening gaps create workplace friction and family conflict. Bridging these differences requires adapting your listening style to the speaker's norms.
takeaways: Each generation has distinct communication preferences
Mismatched styles create misunderstandings across age groups
Adapting your listening approach bridges generational gaps

faq.question: How does technology change listening across generations?
faq.answer: Older generations often feel disrespected by texting during conversations, while younger generations see quick digital responses as attentive. Virtual communication feels natural to digital natives but draining to those who grew up with in-person norms. Neither is wrong; they are different.

faq.question: What is the biggest cross-generational listening mistake?
faq.answer: Assuming your communication style is the correct one and judging others by it. A Boomer dismissing a Gen Z employee as disengaged because they communicate through chat, or a Gen Z worker finding meetings pointless, both reflect style bias rather than substance problems.
